meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Who decided to give my son a zero before anyone called me?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Conclusive. Turnitin's own guide says its score shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student, and I have it printed in my bag. So I'll ask again: who decided, and was anyone going to call me first?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Then what else do you have besides a machine's number?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58. People write somewhere else and paste it into the final document, Hale. That shows me when it arrived, not who wrote it.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Editions differ, and students misquote. Is that line anywhere in the play, in any act?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their minds between an outline and an essay; that's what an outline is for. And you skipped my question about the line.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Five minutes with a seventeen-year-old who'd been cornered after class, no parent there, written up by the person accusing him. That's your impression, not a document. Hand me the September page.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, and I want it in writing tonight, private, nothing on file. Owen does the rewrite to put this behind him, not because of anything in that essay. And the new mark is in the gradebook before December 1.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday the 12th, after school, and your email tonight with all of it in writing, Hale.
Do we have an agreement?
A private supervised rewrite this Thursday after school, the mark replaces the zero before December 1, nothing on his record, and all of it in your email tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Dear Hale,

You agreed to a private supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 this Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero before December 1 and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still expect written confirmation of each of those terms, along with confirmation that nothing about this essay is on his record now. I expect that email from you tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and accepted a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, with the mark replacing the zero before December 1 and nothing on his record; she still wants all of it confirmed in writing tonight, and that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4.
What moved her: You opened the play to Act 3, Scene 2 and let her look for the invented line herself, because that was evidence she could check with her own eyes rather than take on your word.
What cost ground: You opened by calling the 94% checker score conclusive, which handed her the one argument she had come prepared to win.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history from 11:31 to 11:58 PM on the night before the deadline landed very close to that late night, which is why she wrote the times down and went straight to the paste defence; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked whether the line appeared anywhere in the play in any act, answer that question directly before moving on to the outline, so her defence is closed rather than left open for her email.
